files.lesson.md: --- order: 12 unit: chance node: AC9M8P02 n1 uses: [AC9M8P01 n1, AC9M7P01 n1] title: Grids and tree diagrams summary: "Two events, one after the other, make a sample space of pairs. A grid or a tree diagram lists every pair once, so you can count the outcomes in an event and find its probability." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A game asks you to toss a coin and roll a dice: you win with heads and an even number. Is that a good chance or a poor one? First you need every way the two can land." connection: survey-two-way # data/connections/maths.yml (pilot: Make on paper and Also used in; documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8330 url: http://127.0.0.1:8330/index.html readySelector: "#gsum" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: ev.yml#explain-pic, caption: "A coin then a dice: 2 branches, then 6 from each, makes 12 outcomes. Tails and more than 4: 2 of them." } explainClip: query: { code: "@ev.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "A tree diagram" say: "Each branch of the first event splits into every outcome of the second." clip: - caption: { text: "The coin: H or T. Each splits into the dice's 6 outcomes.", say: "Heads or tails, then each splits six ways." } - wait: 1400 - caption: { text: "2 × 6 = 12 outcomes. Tails and more than 4: T 5, T 6.", say: "Twelve outcomes. Tails and more than four: two of them." } - click: "T and 5" - click: "T and 6" - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "2/12" } - wait: 1500 --- When two things happen one after the other (toss a coin, then roll a dice), each outcome is a **pair**, such as (H, 4). A **tree diagram** draws the first event's outcomes as branches, then splits every branch into the second event's outcomes. A **grid** puts the first event down the side and the second across the top: it is a two-way table of the outcomes. ## Predict: how many outcomes? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a count for a coin then a dice shows whether they multiply or add." check: type: predict q: "You toss a coin and roll a dice. How many different outcomes are there?" options: ["8", "6", "12"] actual: "12. Each of the 2 coin results goes with each of the 6 dice results: 2 × 6 = 12 pairs." ``` ## Run: heads and an even number ```step stage: run insight: "Choosing outcomes in the grid and in the tree shows both list the same 12 pairs, so the count is the same." try: { playground: board, starter: "ev.yml#run", height: 620 } check: { type: board, text: "Choose every outcome with heads and an even number. Then press Show as a tree: are they the same outcomes? Was your count of outcomes right?", when: "r = 1", explain: "(H, 2), (H, 4) and (H, 6): 3 of 12, so the probability is 3/12 = 1/4." } ``` ## Investigate: list every pair ```step stage: investigate insight: "Multiply to count pairs; HT and TH are different outcomes, so merging them makes unequal outcomes look equal (Max); trees suit more than two stages." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A spinner has 3 colours and a dice has 6 faces. How many outcomes when you spin, then roll?" answer: 18 tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["9", "Each colour goes with every face: multiply."] explain: "3 × 6 = 18 pairs." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#max" text: "Max finds the chance of one head and one tail with two coins. Click the line where he goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: pairs-order explain: "Line 2: one of each can happen two ways, HT and TH. The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT, so P(one of each) = 2/4 = 1/2." - check: type: question q: "You toss three coins. Which is the best way to list the outcomes?" options: ["A tree diagram", "A grid", "A Venn diagram", "A list of the totals"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A grid has only two directions.", "A Venn diagram sorts one group by properties; it doesn't list pairs.", "Totals hide the outcomes: HHT, HTH and THH all have two heads."] explain: "A tree can keep branching: a column of branches for each event, 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 outcomes." ``` ### Count the pairs Here is the routine. ```worked \text{Spinner with equal red and blue parts};\ \text{then a coin} :: Two events, one after the other. \text{red} \to \text{H, T};\ \text{blue} \to \text{H, T} :: Split each branch into every outcome of the second. 2 \times 2 = 4 \text{ outcomes} :: Count the leaves of the tree. P(\text{blue, H}) = \tfrac{1}{4} :: One leaf out of four. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Max's working. Is "one of each" one outcome, or two? ### Three coins ## Modify: other pairs ```step stage: modify insight: "The same counting on a spinner and coin, two dice and two draws with letters shows a grid or a tree works for any two events." try: { playground: board, starter: "ev.yml#spin", height: 620 } tasks: - starter: "ev.yml#spin" check: { type: board, text: "Spin a spinner with equal red, blue and green parts, then toss a coin. Choose the outcome blue and tails. What is its probability?", when: "r = 1", explain: "1 of 3 × 2 = 6 outcomes: 1/6." } - starter: "ev.yml#dice" hint: "Look along the diagonal where the sums are 8." check: { type: board, text: "Two dice: choose every outcome with a sum of 8.", when: "r = 1", explain: "(2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 3), (6, 2): 5 of 36." } - starter: "ev.yml#same" check: { type: board, text: "A, B or C is picked, put back, then picked again. Choose the outcomes where the same letter comes up twice.", when: "r = 1", explain: "AA, BB and CC: 3 of 9 = 1/3." } - check: type: question q: "Two dice show 36 outcomes in a grid. Why use a grid here, not a tree?" options: ["Trees are only for coins", "36 outcomes fit neatly in a 6 by 6 grid", "A tree can't show dice", "A grid is always better"] answer: 1 feedback: ["Trees work for any events.", null, "A tree can show dice; it just gets large.", "Trees are better for three or more events."] explain: "A tree with 36 leaves is big to draw. Grids suit two events with many outcomes; trees suit two or more events with few outcomes each." ``` ### Spinner and coin ### Sum of 8 ### The same letter ### Grid or tree ## Practise: two events ```step stage: practise insight: "Counting and probabilities for pairs, mixed; listing HT and TH once is the planted slip; Venn diagrams are the review." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Two dice are rolled. What is P(the sum is 7)?" answer: "1/6" feedback: - ["1/11", "The sums 2 to 12 are not equally likely: count the pairs."] explain: "6 of the 36 pairs make 7: 6/36 = 1/6." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "Just the pairs: two dice make a grid with 6 rows and 6 columns. How many pairs is that in all?", answer: 36, tolerance: 0, feedback: [[12, "That's 6 + 6. Each face of one dice goes with every face of the other."]], explain: "6 × 6 = 36 pairs. Now how many of them make 7?" } - check: type: answer q: "Two coins are tossed. What is P(two heads)?" answer: "1/4" feedback: - ["1/3", "HT and TH are different outcomes: there are 4, not 3."] explain: "HH is 1 of the 4 outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT." - check: type: number q: "A café offers 4 sandwiches and 3 drinks. How many different sandwich-and-drink meals are there?" answer: 12 tolerance: 0 explain: "Each sandwich goes with each drink: 4 × 3 = 12." - check: type: number q: "Review: 30 students, 18 play netball, 10 play hockey, 4 play both. How many play neither?" answer: 6 tolerance: 0 explain: "Netball only 14, both 4, hockey only 6: 24. So 30 − 24 = 6." ``` ### Sum of 7 ### Two heads ### Meals ### Review: neither ## Make: a fair game ```step stage: make insight: "Designing an event with probability one half on two dice shows they can count outcomes to a target." try: { playground: board, starter: "ev.yml#make", height: 640 } hint: ["A fair game wins half the time: 18 of 36 outcomes.", "An even sum is one way. Find another."] check: { type: board, text: "Design a two-dice game that you win exactly half the time: choose 18 outcomes.", when: "n = 18", explain: "Any 18 of the 36 outcomes give 1/2, such as 'the sum is even' or 'the first dice is bigger than 3'." } ``` Write the rule of your game in words, then check a friend's game with the grid. ## Make: a survey tree on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A tree for two yes/no survey questions makes them list pairs, keep YN and NY apart, and count an event." hint: ["Two branches first, then two more from each.", "Write each pair at the end of its path."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A form asks each student two questions: 'Do you walk to school?' and 'Do you play a sport?' Each answer is Yes or No. Draw a tree on paper for one student's answers. How many of the pairs of answers have exactly one Yes?" steps: - ["Walk: two branches, Yes and No", "the first question has two answers"] - ["Sport: Yes and No on each branch, so 4 pairs: YY, YN, NY, NN", "every answer to the first goes with every answer to the second"] - ["Exactly one Yes: YN and NY", "these are different pairs: one walks and does not play, the other plays and does not walk"] - ["2 pairs", "two of the four"] picks: - step: 3 q: "Do YN and NY count as two pairs or one?" options: - "Two: they are different answers from different kinds of student" - "One: they have the same letters" - "Only YN counts, because walking is asked first" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The letters match but the pairs do not. Walk-only and sport-only students are different.", "Both orders happen. Neither is left out."] answer: "2" feedback: - ["1", "Yes-No and No-Yes are different pairs: list both."] - ["4", "That is all the pairs. Exactly one Yes leaves out YY and NN."] criteria: - "My tree has two branches, then two more on each." - "I listed all four pairs." - "I counted YN and NY as two different pairs." explain: "The four pairs are YY, YN, NY, NN. Exactly one Yes is YN or NY: 2 pairs." ``` Do this one in your book. A school really can use a form like this, and the answers fill a two-way table. Draw the tree, list the four pairs, and type how many have exactly one Yes. **Also used in** - **Surveys.** The tree for two yes/no questions has the same four cells as the school's two-way table of walkers and sports players. - **Menus and codes.** Two choices on a menu, two coins, and the digits of a code all make pairs, and a tree lists them once. - **Next.** Counting the pairs in an event gives its probability, and the next lesson puts 'and', 'or' and 'not' on the same pictures. ```teacher summary: Students list the outcomes of two events in a grid and a tree diagram, count the outcomes in an event and find its probability (AC9M8P02, node 1). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can list every outcome of two events with a grid or a tree diagram. - I can count the outcomes in an event and give its probability. - I can choose between a grid, a tree and a Venn diagram. struggle: Counting HT and TH as different. Ask students to colour the two coins (a red coin and a blue coin) before they list. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need sample spaces (Year 7) and the Venn diagrams and tables from the last lesson. The one idea: two events make pairs, and a grid or tree lists every pair once, so the outcomes are equally likely. The common mistake is merging pairs that differ only in order (Max's HH, TT, one of each), which makes unequal outcomes look equal. Branch probabilities (multiplying along a tree) are Year 10 (AC9M10P01); here every outcome is equally likely and students count. The board lists outcomes rather than drawing spinners, so the lesson says 'equal parts' every time; point it out. Wider: three coins on a tree (8 outcomes), and why a grid can't show them. running: - "Predict: ask how many dice results go with heads." - "Run: ask whether the grid and tree show the same 12 outcomes." - "Investigate: ask Max to toss a red and a blue coin." - "Modify: ask why the sums of 8 lie on a diagonal." - "Make: ask how many outcomes make a half." - "Paper: the survey tree is worked in books; the page marks the number of pairs with exactly one Yes and the reason YN and NY are different. Books out, and look for four pairs listed, not three." stuck: - see: A student adds the outcomes (2 + 6 = 8). ask: How many dice results go with heads? With tails? fix: "Each first outcome pairs with every second outcome: multiply." - see: A student lists HT and TH once. ask: If one coin is red and one is blue, is red-heads blue-tails the same as red-tails blue-heads? fix: "Order matters: both are outcomes." - see: A student says P(sum is 7) = 1/11. ask: Are the sums 2 to 12 equally likely? fix: Count pairs in the grid, not the list of sums. stretch: "Three coins: draw the tree. What is P(exactly two heads)? Why can't the board's grid show this?" support: A printed 6 by 6 grid for two dice and a blank two-level tree. leads: > This completes AC9M8P02 node 1 with the last lesson. Where it leads: 'and', 'or' and 'not' (next), simulations, and multiplying along branches in Year 10. exit: q: A spinner shows 1, 2 or 3 (equal parts) and a coin is tossed. List the outcomes. What is P(an odd number and heads)? a: "1H, 1T, 2H, 2T, 3H, 3T: 6 outcomes. 1H and 3H, so 2/6 = 1/3." explain: > Two events one after the other make **pairs**. A **tree diagram** splits each first outcome into every second outcome; a **grid** puts one event down the side and the other across. Both list every pair once, so each is equally likely. The number of outcomes is the two counts **multiplied**. Order matters: HT and TH are different outcomes. Then P(event) = outcomes in the event ÷ all outcomes. ```

# Two-event sample spaces as grids and trees, for "Grids and tree diagrams".

# region: run
widget: events
first: coin
second: dice
view: both
target: a = H and b % 2 = 0
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: events
first: coin
second: dice
view: tree
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: events
first: coin
second: dice
view: tree
event: a = T and b > 4
# endregion

# region: spin
widget: events
first: red, blue, green
second: coin
names: Spinner, Coin
view: both
target: a = blue and b = T
# endregion

# region: dice
widget: events
first: dice
second: dice
show: sum
target: s = 8
# endregion

# region: same
widget: events
first: A, B, C
second: A, B, C
names: First letter, Second letter
view: both
target: a = b
# endregion

# region: make
widget: events
first: dice
second: dice
show: sum
# endregion
files.working.txt:
# Max's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: max
Max tosses two coins and lists what can happen.
The equally likely outcomes are: HH, TT, and one of each.
That is 3 outcomes, and one of them is "one of each".
So P(one head and one tail) = 1/3.
# endregion
